front: {{c1::Allostatic load}} is cumulative physiological wear from chronic stress — a key mechanism linking low SES and discrimination to disease.
why: Allostatic load is the named stress mechanism linking SES/discrimination to disease

front: {{c1::Compliance}} implies patient obedience, {{c2::adherence}} implies an agreed plan, and concordance describes shared decision-making about the regimen.
why: Adherence is exam-relevant health behavior; concordance nuance is secondary

front: {{c1::Food deserts}} are areas with poor access to affordable nutritious food, concentrating diet-related disease in low-income and rural communities.
why: Food deserts: named structural access barrier, core social determinant example

front: {{c1::Fundamental cause}} theory (Link and Phelan): SES stays linked to disease across eras because money, knowledge, and networks are flexible resources.
why: Fundamental cause theory is the standard explanation for the persistent SES gradient

front: {{c1::Illness experience}} is the interactionist study of how people manage symptoms, meaning, and identity — central in chronic disease.
why: Illness experience is AAMC-listed (9A health & medicine) but secondary to disparities

front: {{c1::Incidence}} counts new cases arising over a period; {{c2::prevalence}} counts all existing cases at a point in time.
why: Incidence vs prevalence is core epidemiology; back adds the duration relationship

front: {{c1::Lead-time}} bias lengthens measured survival by diagnosing earlier; {{c2::length}} bias makes screening oversample slow-growing disease.
why: Screening biases appear in research-methods passages; second-tier for this topic

front: {{c1::Medicalization}} turns nonmedical problems into illnesses (ADHD, baldness); {{c2::demedicalization}} reverses it — homosexuality left the DSM in 1973.
why: Medicalization is tested (9A); demedicalization/1973 is supporting detail

front: {{c1::Medicare}} covers people 65 and older plus those with ESRD or disability; {{c2::Medicaid}} is joint federal-state coverage based on income.
why: Medicare vs Medicaid is the classic healthcare-access discrete

front: {{c1::Single-payer}} means one entity pays for privately delivered care; {{c2::socialized medicine}} means government also owns facilities and staff.
why: System-type vocabulary; plausible passage context, rarely asked outright

front: {{c1::Social epidemiology}} studies how social structure — class, race, gender, place — distributes disease and mortality across populations.
why: Social epidemiology is a named AAMC concept framing the whole topic

front: A {{c1::DALY}} counts years of healthy life lost to illness and premature death; a {{c2::QALY}} weights years of life gained by their quality.
why: DALY/QALY metrics are not in the AAMC outline; trivia-grade for this section

front: A study finds higher hypertension rates among Black patients and concludes there is a genetic cause. What is the interpretive error?
why: Race as social construct vs genetic explanation is a classic passage reasoning item

front: Ajzen's theory of planned behavior predicts intention from three components. Name them and the model's main limitation.
why: Theory of planned behavior is outside 10A and not in the AAMC outline

front: An uninsured woman in labor arrives at an emergency department. Which law governs the response, and what does it fail to cover?
why: EMTALA is US-policy minutiae; a named law the exam would supply in-passage

front: Being {{c1::uninsured}} or underinsured predicts delayed care, skipped medications, fewer screenings, and later-stage diagnoses.
why: Uninsurance as an access barrier with signature disparity outcomes

front: Beyond cost, what barriers limit healthcare access?
why: Non-cost access barriers are the core healthcare-access content

front: Case and Deaton documented rising midlife mortality among less-educated Americans from three causes. Name them and the proposed mechanism.
why: Named study (Case & Deaton) with specific findings; passage would supply it

front: Contrast the sick role and illness experience.
why: Sick role vs illness experience contrast is tested but belongs to 9A

front: Contrast upstream and downstream interventions for health disparities.
why: Upstream/downstream framing is useful reasoning but rarely a direct question

front: Cultural capital refers to:
why: Cultural capital is tested under social class; tangential to health here

front: Define social determinants of health.
why: Definition of social determinants of health is the topic's anchor concept

front: Discrimination differs from prejudice in being:
why: Prejudice vs discrimination is a tested distinction, though from 8C not 10A

front: Distinguish disease, illness, and sickness.
why: Disease/illness/sickness triad supports sick role and illness experience

front: Distinguish health equality from health equity.
why: Equity vs equality distinction is a definition the exam uses for disparities

front: Distinguish incidence from prevalence.
why: Near-restatement of the incidence/prevalence cloze card in this deck

front: Gender paradox: women show higher {{c1::morbidity}} (illness rates) but lower {{c2::mortality}} — living longer while reporting more sickness.
why: Gender morbidity/mortality paradox is the standard gender-disparity fact

front: How can health disadvantage transmit across generations?
why: Intergenerational transmission supports life-course/SES content as a second step

front: How do physicians act as gatekeepers of the sick role?
why: Physician legitimation of the sick role is supporting detail on the sick role

front: How does implicit bias produce disparities in clinical care?
why: Implicit bias in clinical care is core healthcare-disparities content

front: How does residential segregation affect health?
why: Residential segregation is the key spatial-inequality mechanism for disparities

front: How does stigma affect health and healthcare seeking?
why: Stigma's effect on care-seeking is a frequently tested disparity mechanism

front: How does structural competency go beyond cultural competency in addressing disparities?
why: Structural competency is a useful frame but secondary vocabulary

front: In life-course models, contrast a critical-period effect with an accumulation effect.
why: Critical-period vs accumulation is supporting detail on the life-course model

front: In Parsons's {{c1::sick role}}, the ill are exempted from normal obligations and not blamed, but must want recovery and seek competent help.
why: Parsons' sick role is heavily tested but sits in 9A, not disparities

front: Institutional discrimination operates through:
why: Institutional discrimination is the named AAMC concept behind systemic disparities

front: Limited {{c1::health literacy}} — difficulty obtaining and using health information — impairs navigation and adherence, concentrating in low-SES groups.
why: Health literacy is a named access barrier tied to SES

front: Medicalization can worsen inequality by:
why: Medicalization-inequality link is a plausible second-step inference

front: Meyer's {{c1::minority stress}} model explains sexual and gender minority health gaps via stigma, concealment, and {{c2::internalized}} stigma.
why: Minority stress model explains SGM disparities; named but passage-plausible

front: Name the constructs of the Health Belief Model that predict whether a patient takes a preventive action.
why: Health Belief Model constructs appear in health-behavior passages

front: Physicians shown identical actor-patients describing chest pain referred Black women for catheterization less often. What does this design establish?
why: Experimental isolation of provider bias supports the implicit-bias card

front: Social capital contributes to health by:
why: Social capital is tested under social class; health link is secondary

front: Stages of change: precontemplation, {{c1::contemplation}}, preparation, action, {{c2::maintenance}}, with relapse expected rather than a failure.
why: Stages of change is common health-behavior passage material

front: The {{c1::life-course}} perspective: health reflects accumulating exposures from gestation onward, with sensitive periods and chains of risk.
why: Life-course perspective is a supporting frame for SES-health mechanisms

front: The {{c1::SES gradient}} in health: outcomes improve at every step up the socioeconomic ladder, not merely above a poverty threshold.
why: The SES gradient (not just poverty threshold) is the section's central relationship

front: The {{c1::weathering}} hypothesis: chronic stress from racism accelerates physiological aging among Black Americans, worsening outcomes at earlier ages.
why: Weathering hypothesis: named but frequently supplied in race-disparity passages

front: The Hispanic paradox refers to:
why: Hispanic paradox is a second-tier disparity example seen in prep and passages

front: What are the main mechanisms linking low SES to poor health?
why: Mechanisms linking SES to health outcomes are the core of 10A

front: What are the major criticisms of Parsons's sick role?
why: Sick-role criticism (chronic illness) is a common test point, though 9A

front: What characterizes the rural mortality penalty in the US?
why: US rural mortality specifics are encyclopedic; access barriers already covered

front: What did the Whitehall studies demonstrate?
why: Named study; the SES gradient cloze already covers Whitehall in its back

front: What distinguishes cultural humility from cultural competence?
why: Cultural humility vs competence is vocabulary not in the AAMC outline

front: What explains men's higher mortality despite women's higher morbidity?
why: Near-restatement of the gender paradox card's back

front: What explains the roughly twofold Black-white infant mortality gap in the US?
why: Infant mortality gap is the classic race-disparity example with structural reasoning

front: What forces drive medicalization?
why: Drivers of medicalization are encyclopedic detail beyond the tested definition

front: What happens to care quality when patients with limited English proficiency do not receive a professional interpreter?
why: LEP interpreter outcomes are supporting detail on language access barriers

front: What is medicalization?
why: Near-restatement of the medicalization cloze card

front: What is the difference between health equity and equality?
why: Near-restatement of the equity vs equality card

front: What is the epidemiological transition?
why: Epidemiological transition pairs with demographic transition; plausible stem

front: What is the inverse care law?
why: Inverse care law is a named concept that surfaces in access passages

front: What is the social gradient in health?
why: Near-restatement of the SES gradient cloze card

front: Which study design suits a rare disease, and which one lets you compute incidence?
why: Study-design basics are research-methods content; useful epi second step

front: Why can improved medical technology sometimes WIDEN disparities?
why: Technology widening disparities is a direct fundamental-cause prediction

front: Why have race coefficients been removed from eGFR and pulmonary function equations?
why: eGFR/PFT race-coefficient removal is clinical-policy minutiae; race-as-social covered
